analysis.one_liner: Requires equal pay for jobs of equivalent skill, regardless of the worker's sex, race, or national origin.
analysis.headline: The bill has received no action and no cosponsors since being referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on May 4, 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would extend federal equal-pay law beyond "equal work" to "equivalent jobs," so an employer could not pay lower wages in a job dominated by women or by racial or ethnic minorities than it pays in a different job that requires comparable skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions. It would let workers recover back pay plus compensatory and punitive damages, sue as a class with expert fees paid, protect employees who discuss wages from retaliation, and require employers with 25 or more employees (15 or more in later years) to report wages by sex, race, and national origin to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. It would also apply these rules to congressional and executive branch employees. Introduced by DC's non-voting delegate with no cosponsors, it sits in committee with no action taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Women and workers of color in jobs that are dominated by their sex, race, or national origin and pay less than equivalent jobs dominated by men or white workers — such as many care, service, and administrative roles. They would gain the right to back pay, compensatory and punitive damages, class actions with expert fees, and protection from retaliation for comparing wages. Employees of Congress and the executive branch would get the same protections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women and workers of color in undervalued jobs

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for an employer to pay lower wages in a job dominated by one sex, race, or national origin than it pays in an equivalent job dominated by another, closing the gap between the current "equal work" standard and jobs that are dissimilar but comparable in skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions.
Gives workers stronger remedies: back pay treated as unpaid wages, plus compensatory or punitive damages, expert fees for prevailing plaintiffs, and the option to sue as a class action.
Makes it unlawful for employers to fire or otherwise punish an employee for asking about, disclosing, or discussing wages — the transparency workers need to discover a pay gap in the first place.

Requires employers with 25 or more employees (15 or more in later years) to file wage reports with the EEOC broken down by sex, race, and national origin, while protecting employee confidentiality — giving regulators and the public the data to spot patterns of pay discrimination.
Bars employers from complying by cutting anyone's wages, and applies the same rules to congressional employees and executive branch staff, so the law covers Congress's own workplaces.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — especially those with workforces concentrated by sex, race, or national origin — would bear the cost of documenting how they set wages, filing EEOC wage reports, and paying back wages and damages where a court finds pay discrimination between equivalent jobs. The federal government, as a large employer, would share enforcement and compliance costs (though not punitive damages).

drawbacks.text: The "equivalent jobs" standard requires comparing dissimilar jobs, which is genuinely hard to do: the EEOC must define when a job is "dominated" by a group, and courts would have to weigh skills, effort, and responsibility across very different roles — inviting expensive litigation over subjective job valuations.

The bill's own findings attribute 62% of the wage gap to occupational and industry differences, experience, education, and other factors, leaving 38% unexplained — so the remedy targets that residual share while imposing recordkeeping and reporting duties on all covered employers.

Covered employers would face new compliance burdens — preserving wage-setting records, filing detailed wage reports by race and sex — plus exposure to compensatory and punitive damages, costs that fall hardest on employers in sectors with segregated workforces.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers in systematically undervalued jobs, the bill offers real money: back pay, damages, and a legal standard that reaches the pay gap between female-dominated and male-dominated work that the 1963 Equal Pay Act does not touch. The costs are real too — the equivalent-jobs standard is administratively complex, depends heavily on EEOC rulemaking that does not yet exist, and would generate compliance costs and litigation across covered employers. An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill is ambitious and untested: whether it delivers wage gains or mainly litigation depends entirely on regulations and court decisions that have not been written.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2026 and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which has taken no further action; it has no cosponsors and has not received a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the Fair Pay Act of 2026 in the House on May 4, 2026.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, where it has remained with no hearings, markup, or vote scheduled.
No member of the House — from either party — has signed on as a cosponsor, and the only sponsor is a delegate who cannot vote on final passage.
Congress remains in session through January 3, 2027, so the bill is technically alive but shows none of the support that would move it forward.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced new pay-equity liability, damages exposure, and wage-reporting duties are better off so far, because the bill has not advanced. Workers in undervalued jobs have gained nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have faced new liability

for.name: Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action since — no hearing, markup, or vote

against.name: House members of both parties
against.role: 219 House Democrats and 223 House Republicans (all voting members)
against.what_they_did: None signed on as cosponsors, leaving the bill with a single non-voting sponsor

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred and no member of either party cosponsored the bill, so there is no record yet of where the parties stand — only that it has drawn zero support from 217 Democrats and 223 Republicans alike.

industries.industry: Employers with sex- or race-segregated workforces (retail, health care, hospitality, care work, administrative services)
industries.note: These employers could no longer pay female- or minority-dominated jobs less than equivalent male- or white-dominated jobs, and would owe back pay and damages where courts find violations. Their savings from lower wages in undervalued jobs are exactly what the bill would take away from them and give to workers.

industries.industry: Covered employers with 25 or more employees (15 or more in later years)
industries.note: They would have to preserve records of how wages are set and file annual EEOC reports disclosing wage rates by sex, race, and national origin. The public gains visibility into pay patterns; employers gain new compliance and disclosure duties.

industries.industry: Federal government as an employer (Congress and the executive branch)
industries.note: The bill applies the same equivalent-pay rules to congressional employees and executive branch staff, so Congress's own workplaces would be subject to the standard it imposes on private employers. The government would also bear the cost of administering the program, though it is shielded from punitive damages.

analysis.trajectory: With a single non-voting sponsor, zero cosponsors, and a Republican-controlled committee that has taken no action, the bill is on the standard path to dying quietly in committee when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027 — like the comparable pay-equity bills Norton has introduced in past Congresses.
